title: Veterans tax credit, set by your town
summary: New Hampshire guarantees only $50 off your property tax, but a town may adopt an optional credit of up to $750, rising to $1,000 from April 2027. What you actually get depends entirely on where you live.
amount: A standard credit of $50, or an optional credit a town may adopt of $51 up to $750. From 1 April 2027 the optional range rises to $51 up to $1,000.
eligibility: You are a resident of New Hampshire and a Veteran as defined in RSA 21:50

Under the all Veterans credit, you served not less than 90 days on active service in the armed forces and continue to serve, or were discharged of a character outlined in RSA 21:50, or are an officer who continues to serve or was honorably separated
A spouse or surviving spouse of such a resident may also qualify
Towns adopt the all Veterans credit separately, under RSA 72:28-b
details: The credit is subtracted from the property tax itself, not from assessed value, so the full amount comes off your bill.
The optional credit replaces the standard credit entirely rather than adding to it. So in a town that has adopted $750, you receive $750, not $800.

There is a scheduled increase worth knowing about. The optional ceiling is $750 until 1 April 2027, and $1,000 from that date. If your town is considering an increase, that is the number to ask about.

The all Veterans credit at RSA 72:28-b matters because it removed the wartime service requirement. Where a town adopts it, the amount is the same as whatever standard or optional credit that town already has under RSA 72:28. A town that had an existing credit before 18 August 2016 may phase the all Veterans credit in over three years to match.

Because every meaningful amount depends on local adoption, two Veterans in neighbouring towns can receive $50 and $750 for identical service. Ask your town assessor which credits your town has adopted.
A surviving spouse of a resident who suffered a service-connected death may apply the credit against any real property in the same municipality where they live, not only the former home.
New Hampshire has no general income tax on wages, so there is no military retirement question here.
agency: Town and city assessors, under credits adopted locally per RSA 72:27-a
statuteRef: RSA 72:28, with the all Veterans credit at RSA 72:28-b

title: Tax credit for service-connected total disability
summary: A Veteran with total and permanent service-connected disability gets a standard $700 credit, and a town may raise it to as much as $5,000. Read the interaction carefully, because the optional version replaces several other benefits.
amount: A standard yearly credit of $700, or an optional credit a town may adopt of $701 up to $5,000
eligibility: You were discharged of a character outlined in RSA 21:50, or are an officer honorably separated from military service
And you have total and permanent service-connected disability
Or you are a double amputee or paraplegic because of a service-connected injury
A surviving spouse of such a person also qualifies
details: The credit is subtracted from the property tax on your residential property each year.

Here is the interaction to understand before your town adopts anything. The statute says the optional credit for service-connected permanent and total disability replaces the credits under RSA 72:28, 72:28-b, 72:28-c and RSA 72:36-a in their entirety, and is not in addition to them.

That last one is significant, because RSA 72:36-a is the full exemption from all taxation for a specially adapted home. On the face of the text, a Veteran in a town with the optional disability credit would receive that credit instead of the full exemption. If you hold an SAH or SHA adapted home, raise this with your assessor directly rather than assuming, because the difference could be large in either direction.
The gap between the standard $700 and the $5,000 ceiling is the widest local variation in the state, so which town you live in matters more here than anywhere else.

title: Full exemption for a specially adapted home
summary: If the VA adapted your home through an SAH or SHA grant, New Hampshire exempts that homestead from all taxation. Individual unemployability counts, and so does a home bought with the proceeds of selling an adapted one.
amount: Exempt from all taxation on the homestead
eligibility: You are a Veteran as defined by RSA 21:50
And you own a home specially adapted by the Veterans Administration through an approved Special Adapted Housing or Special Home Adaptation grant
Or you own a home that has been specially adapted and was acquired using proceeds from the sale of such an SAH or SHA home
And you are 100 percent permanently and totally disabled as prescribed in 38 C.F.R. 3.340, which covers total and permanent total ratings and unemployability
Or you are a double amputee of the upper or lower extremities, or any combination, or paraplegic, as a result of service connection
Or you have blindness of both eyes with visual acuity of 5/200 or less as a result of service connection
A surviving spouse as defined in RSA 72:29, V also qualifies
details: Unemployability is covered. The statute points to 38 C.F.R. 3.340, which expressly includes unemployability, so a Veteran paid at the 100 percent rate through TDIU falls inside this.
The provision for a home bought with the proceeds of selling an adapted home is easy to miss and means you do not lose the exemption by moving, provided the new home is also specially adapted.
You have to furnish satisfactory proof of the service connection disability to the assessors.

Check the interaction with RSA 72:35 before relying on this. Where a town has adopted the optional service-connected total disability credit, the statute says that credit replaces this exemption entirely. Ask your assessor which applies in your town.
This section was amended again with effect from 31 August 2026, so make sure any guidance you read post-dates that.
